author: cskiraly
content:
Ok, so SEACAST was developed for segmented message broadcast and sampled diffusion.
1. first use case was blobs (I gues people remember that). At the time it was stil a predecessor of the protocol called FullDAS. Around the same time we also did PeerDAS. Than we introduced cell-level messaging, and batch publish. For all these, we choose to map them on GossipSub topics, because that was what people wanted at the time. The protocols themselves were mostly defined indepedent of that mapping.
2. next use case was Payload (and it's BAL containing variant, and the variant where the Payload and the BAL are separated, but both segmented).
3. The use case after that is the aggregates (the proofs), what you are looking for here. That's what we are studying now.

There will be next steps. We foresee them. From the networking point they are all very similar, although the traffic patterns themselves are different which does require adaptation. Hence, we don't start from scratch each time. They are also all CL (for now, we will have EL later, but that doesn't belong here):
- the consensus block: I'm already testing the segmentation of this
- ZK proofs: when it comes, we will want to segment them. We alrady know
- sampled payload: this will arrive too, we just don't do it yet because we are delaying ZK rollout

We are thinking in perspective, at least I try to do. I think there is some underlying essence missing from some of the quesitons here, Good protocols that stand the test of times are usually not just working in one very specific setting. That's what we are doing here from the networking perspective, designing protocols that are flexible enough to accomodate these use cases and traffic patterns, and finding the settings that match the specific use case.

author: cskiraly
content: Do not confuse this with complexity. You can easily specify a protocol, test it in realistic looking settings , it works, and it still doesn't have the basics, such as timeouts. There are basics that we should ensure are there for the protocol to survive in adverse conditions. These seemingly "add" complexity, but you just have to have them.

author: cskiraly
content: As an update, I'm working towards simulations (with go seacast code) with 10K nodes, with proof segmentation (and payload segmentation, but we can turn that off it that's the desire).

author: cskiraly
content:
I know many just want numbers, and I think it is the right thing in this forum, but it is important to understand that in the background we are ironing out details that make huge differences in those numbers, and decide how much you can trust them. One example is here: https://notes.ethereum.org/@cskiraly/EIP-8411-shadow-cross-check#4-Queue-order-explains-the-baseline-gap-and-part-of-Cs-advantage
The number easily differ by 30-40% based on how we run these things. 

Obviously you don't have to see all these details, but we have to make quite some work to have reliable numbers. That's why to some questions, as much as I would love to explain the details, I have to answer "let us figure it out in a networking forum", where people are interested in the detail.
